title: Pint
description: Unit of volume in the imperial and US systems
wiki_lead:
The pint (, ; symbol pt, sometimes abbreviated as p) is a unit of volume or capacity in both the imperial and United States customary measurement systems. In both of those systems, it is one-eighth of a gallon. 
The British imperial pint is 20.095% larger than the US pint because the two systems are defined differently as the British completely reorganized and defined the current imperial system in 1824 whereas the US system is derived from earlier English unit systems. Almost all other countries have standardized on the metric system, so although several still have units called pints or are otherwise based on ounces (such as for beverages), the volume varies by regional custom.
The imperial pint (≈ 568 mL) is used in the United Kingdom, other Commonwealth countries and Ireland. In the United States, two kinds of pint are used: a liquid pint (≈ 473 mL) and a less common dry pint (≈ 551 mL). 
Other former British colonies, such as Australia, South Africa and New Zealand, converted to the metric system in the 1960s and 1970s, so while the term pint may still be in common use in these countries, it may no longer refer to the British imperial pint once used throughout the British Empire.

Almost all other countries have standardized on the metric system, so although several still have units called pints or are otherwise based on ounces (such as for beverages), the volume varies by regional custom.
The imperial pint (≈ 568 mL) is used in the United Kingdom, other Commonwealth countries and Ireland. In the United States, two kinds of pint are used: a liquid pint (≈ 473 mL) and a less common dry pint (≈ 551 mL). 
Other former British colonies, such as Australia, South Africa and New Zealand, converted to the metric system in the 1960s and 1970s, so while the term pint may still be in common use in these countries, it may no longer refer to the British imperial pint once used throughout the British Empire.


Name

Pint comes from the Old French word pinte and perhaps ultimately from Vulgar Latin pincta meaning "painted", for marks painted on the side of a container to show capacity.
In France, the French word pinte is now used to describe a half-litre, slightly smaller than an Imperial pint, but in Canadian French it is used to describe an Imperial quart and the French word chopine is used for an Imperial pint.


Definitions


Imperial pint
The imperial pint is equal to one-eighth of an imperial gallon of exactly 4.54609 L, i.e. 568.26125 millilitres.

The liquid pint is legally defined as one-eighth of a gallon of exactly 231 cubic inches, i.e. 28.875 cubic inches or 473.176473 millilitres.

In the United States, the dry pint is equal to ⁠1/64⁠ of a US bushel of exactly 2150.42 cubic inches, i.e. 33.6003125 cubic inches or 550.6104713575 milliltres.


Other pints

The Scottish pint or joug, an obsolete Scottish unit, is equal to 1696 mL (2.93 Imperial pints). It remained in use until 1826, surviving significantly longer than most other old Scottish measurements.
The word pint is one of numerous false friends between English and French. They are not the same unit although they have the same linguistic origin. The French word pinte is etymologically related, but historically described a larger unit. grok_lead: The pint is a unit of volume or capacity historically used for measuring liquids such as beer, milk, and cider in both the imperial and United States customary systems of measurement. In the imperial system, as codified in United Kingdom legislation, the pint is defined exactly as 0.56826125 cubic decimetres, equivalent to 568.26125 millilitres or 20 imperial fluid ounces. In the US customary system, the liquid pintâdistinguished from the slightly larger dry pintâis defined as exactly 28.875 cubic inches, equivalent to 473.176473 millilitres or 16 US fluid ounces. This volume discrepancy, stemming from separate standardizations in the 19th century, means an imperial pint exceeds a US liquid pint by about 20%, a fact that has practical implications for international trade and consumer expectations in serving sizes. The unit traces its origins to medieval European measures, with the term deriving from the Old French "pinte," referring to marks painted on containers to indicate capacity, and was formalized as one-eighth of a gallon based on weights of commodities like wheat. Standardization efforts in the UK under the Weights and Measures Act and in the US via federal specifications addressed prior variability, yet the pint persists amid metrication pressures due to cultural entrenchment, particularly in pub servings of draught beer where UK law mandates the pint as an authorized unit. Controversies include debates over short-measuring in hospitality and resistance to abolishing the pint for alcohol, as empirical studies indicate its removal could reduce consumption volumes. In the US, dry pints apply to commodities like blueberries, while liquid pints feature in dairy and brewing contexts.
